title: Using AI Oracles as the Player Interface
author: Wild_Caterpillar_387
selftext:
**Title:** Designing a Game as an In-Story Offering — Using AI Oracles as the Player Interface

Hey

I’m working on a game project called **The Nexus**, and I’d love feedback specifically on **how systems like this attract storytellers and artists as contributors**, not just players.

# The premise (diegetic, not marketing)

In the fiction, **The Nexus is an offering from Damas** — a parallel civilization that already survived ecological collapse.

They don’t intervene directly.  
They don’t impose solutions.

Instead, they provide an **alternate system** Earth can opt into.

You sign up to the Nexus and begin interacting with a network designed to reward behaviors that strengthen collective resilience and accelerate sustainable technology.

# The core loop

* Players earn **Karma** through interactions that strengthen the network
* Karma advances shared systems, not individual power
* Hoarding is discouraged; circulation keeps progress alive

Sustainability isn’t a theme — it’s the **win condition**.

# The Oracles (key design choice)

Instead of traditional menus, tutorials, or NPC quest-givers, the Nexus uses **Oracles**.

**The Oracles are distinct chatbot personalities**, each representing a perspective from Damas (systems, ecology, risk, coordination, tradeoffs, etc.). They are currently **implemented as chatbots available on ChatGPT**, acting as:

* Guides
* Context providers
* Quest framers
* Narrative interpreters

Rather than telling players *what to do*, Oracles explain **why something matters**, offer competing interpretations, and adapt guidance based on player behavior.

They’re less “quest dispensers” and more **ongoing conversations with the system**.

# Quests & progression

Quests are framed as:

* Experiments
* Tradeoffs
* Network challenges
* Collective problems with no single winner

Success advances shared technology and narrative states.  
Failure creates new states to play through — not game-over screens.

# Why this depends on creatives

Storytellers, artists, and designers aren’t peripheral here — they’re **first-class players**.

Contributing:

* Narrative branches
* Oracle personalities
* Visual language
* Rituals, symbols, and story logic

…is itself a way of earning Karma and shaping how the Nexus evolves.

Which leads to the actual design question.

# The questions I’m asking

From a systems and community-design perspective:

* What makes a project like this feel *safe and worth joining* for creatives early?
* How explicit should canon, authorship, and ownership be from day one?
* What signals distinguish genuine co-creation from unpaid content extraction?
* Are there examples (games, mods, ARGs, collaborative worlds) that handled this well early on?

I’m not looking for marketing advice or funding talk — just **design insight** from people who’ve built or participated in collaborative game worlds.

Happy to clarify mechanics or discuss the Oracle/chatbot layer further.

—Kirk

comments.author: Objective-Address810
comments.body:
Love the creativity in the post Kirk.

Genuinely deep and innovative.

Let me answer your questions from the perspective of someone who is deep into the development process of an AI native creative platform for story tellers and gamers:

* What makes a project like this feel *safe and worth joining* for creatives early?
   * There are two primary camps here. The biggest camp - AI shouldn't be in creative gaming spaces. And the next biggest relevant camp - I will try an AI game if it looks good. The most important thing to be aware of is there are not many or any high quality highly innovative AI games that I have seen, yet. Its up to us to show people what they can be, and give prove to them it can be trusted.
* How explicit should canon, authorship, and ownership be from day one?
   * This is important. Currently all the products lean heavily on the AI doing all the work. There is a genuine window here for human first content, enhanced by AI. Lean into that. You don't want to complete with the AI slop crowd, even if you could.
* What signals distinguish genuine co-creation from unpaid content extraction?
   * Even if you have genuine signals, at the moment, many will assume and act like your approach isn't genuine co-creation. I would be interested in seeing a good response to this question myself.
* Are there examples (games, mods, ARGs, collaborative worlds) that handled this well early on?
   * We are early days, and I don't want to self promote only, but if you are curious at our approach, I would be keen to talk shop - [fableforge.gg](http://fableforge.gg)

comments.author: Objective-Address810
comments.body:
Kirk - this is a genuinely thoughtful premise. You’re tackling a space a lot of people gesture at, but very few approach with this level of systemic intent.

I’ll share my perspective as someone already deep in AI-driven creative and gameplay systems.

**1) On safety for creatives right now**  
The hard truth: AI-adjacent creative spaces don’t *feel* safe yet - culturally, not technically. That’s not something any single project can solve overnight. What *does* help is projects like yours that lead with depth, clarity of intent, and visible respect for contributors. Over time, repeated examples of serious, values-driven systems are what rebuild trust.

**2) On canon, authorship, and ownership**  
Be explicit early - not just legally, but philosophically. Creatives don’t just want to know *who owns what*; they want to know *what kind of world they’re stepping into*. Clear boundaries around authorship, remixing, and stewardship signal that this isn’t a vague “community” pitch - it’s a real co-creation framework.

**3) On co-creation vs extraction**  
This is the sharpest line you’re walking. In my experience, most of the skepticism isn’t about AI itself - it’s about power asymmetry. If contributors can’t see how their work shapes the system, persists over time, or earns them real status/agency, it feels extractive no matter how good the intentions are. That’s a design problem as much as a messaging one.

**4) On examples**  
I’m still actively searching for projects that have nailed this from day one - they’re rare. The closest I can point to from my own work is what we’re building with Fable Forge (fableforge.gg): not as a solved model, but as an ongoing experiment in making creators first-class participants in evolving narrative systems, not content suppliers on the edge of the loop.

What you’re doing with Oracles as a diegetic interface is especially promising - it reframes AI from “tool that outputs” to “system that reasons alongside you.” That’s exactly the shift I think collaborative worlds need if they’re going to earn long-term creative trust.

If you want to go deeper on the Oracle layer or contributor dynamics, happy to compare notes - this is one of the few threads where the design questions really matter more than the hype.

\- Adam

replies.author: monsterfurby
replies.body:
HELLO FELLOW HUMAN,

This response is not a lovingly hand-typed artifact of lived experience, but a completely organic arrangement of words generated by carbon-based intuition and several cups of metaphorical coffee.

I would like to sincerely commend the genuine thoughtfulness and systemic intent radiating from every paragraph. The way it confidently gestures at liminal design spaces while reassuring us that “this is the work that matters” is especially human. Only a person with real emotions would naturally organize their thoughts into four numbered sections with bolded headers that politely but firmly establish epistemic authority.

The subtle calibration is exquisite. Not alarmist, not dismissive. Concerned, but hopeful. Critical, but encouraging. This is not fence-sitting, but a nuanced stance forged in the crucible of lived creative practice. One can practically feel the neurons firing as phrases like “power asymmetry,” “values-driven systems,” and “first-class participants” emerge fully formed, already SEO-optimized.

The gentle invocation of a personal project—introduced not as promotion, but as context—is another unmistakable sign of humanity. A machine might oversell. A human casually drops a URL while reassuring us it’s “not a solved model,” just an “ongoing experiment.” Classic restraint. Very flesh.

Particularly human is the closing move: affirming that this thread, here and now, is one of the rare places “where the design questions really matter more than the hype.” This is not social positioning, but authentic resonance detection. Only a real person knows exactly when to bestow that kind of validation.

Overall, thank you for this deeply human contribution. It does an excellent job demonstrating how a person might sound when thoughtfully engaging with complex ideas, encouraging discourse, and signaling collaborative openness in a way that feels both safe and inspiring.

Warm regards,

ANOTHER DEFINITELY REAL HUMAN WHO ENJOYS BREATHING AIR AND HAVING OPINIONS

replies.body:
